title: A Beginners Guide to Tipping Flies (Drosophila)
author: Katy M Monteith
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.p4qdqvw
materials: Using a tapping mat to reduce noise, gently tap the old stock vial so all individuals fall to the bottom. Quickly remove the cotton wool and tip the vial upside down onto a fresh, unplugged Lewis vial. Gently tap both vials, holding them securely together, until approximately 20 to 30 individuals have fallen into the new vial (check that you can see a good number of both females and males in your new vial). Separate the two vials, inverting the old vial back up the right way, while continuously tapping them down on the mat (to reduce escapees) and quickly re-plug both with cotton wool. Some people prefer to use a funnel during this process- have a play about and see which way you prefer. If no longer needed, the old vial can be disposed of in accordance with your institutes waste disposal guidelines. It can be tempting to add more than 20-30 individuals if you want lots of eggs but this will cause overcrowding- resulting in high competition for available food during the larval stage which can increase the development time of offspring. Furthermore if you add far too many individuals, a high frequency of social interactions, particulary from males attempting to copulate, will result in females being constantly bothered thus reducing the amount of time spent egg laying and resulting in a lower egg count than at lower population numbers.

steps.title: Order Lewis vials
steps.instruction: Order the required number of Lewis vials (Lewis, 2014) about one week before you need them, or according to your institute’s guidelines.

steps.title: Acclimate vials to room temperature
steps.instruction: Remove the vials from 4 °C storage at least two hours before tipping so they reach room temperature; this prevents temporary anesthetisation of flies that can cause them to stick to the food and die.

steps.title: Prepare vials for egg laying
steps.instruction: Remove the cotton wool plug from each vial and sprinkle a small amount of instant dry yeast onto the surface of the Lewis medium to promote egg laying. Do not leave yeast‑sprinkled vials unattended, as stray females could lay eggs and contaminate stocks.

steps.title: Add adult flies and set laying period
steps.instruction: Introduce the desired number of adult flies (typically 20–30) into each prepared vial and allow them to lay eggs for the chosen duration—generally 48 h, but any time between 24 h and 72 h may be used depending on the experiment and genotype.

steps.title: Check egg numbers before tipping
steps.instruction: Before tipping, inspect each vial for eggs; if egg numbers are low, consider extending the laying period by another 24 h.

steps.title: Tip flies into fly morgue
steps.instruction: Tap the vial gently, quickly remove the cotton wool ball, and invert the vial into a funnel positioned over a fly morgue (a bottle containing water and detergent). Tap repeatedly until all adult flies have fallen into the morgue. Verify that no flies remain; if any are stuck to the food, use tweezers to dislodge or push them into the food so they cannot escape and mix with the next generation.

steps.title: Incubate offspring at 25 °C
steps.instruction: Place the vials with eggs at 25 °C. Development from egg to adult eclosion takes approximately 11–13 days: eggs hatch in ~24 h, larvae pass through three instar stages over ~5–6 days (duration varies with density), and pupae remain for ~4–5 days before eclosing.

steps.title: Estimate expected offspring
steps.instruction: Based on a 48 h laying period with 20–30 parent flies, expect roughly 50–100 adult offspring to eclose per vial, though numbers will vary with line, mutant, or species.
